title: Book 8, Chapter 24 — Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of the War—Revolt of Ionia— Intervention of Persia—The War in Ionia
paragraphs: When the news reached Athens, for a long while they refused to believe even the most respected of the soldiers who had themselves escaped from the scene of action and clearly reported the matter — a destruction so complete being thought incredible. When the conviction was forced on them, they were angry with the orators who had joined in promoting the expedition, just as if they had not voted for it themselves, and were furious too with the reciters of oracles and soothsayers and all the other omen-mongers of the time who had encouraged them to hope they would conquer Sicily. Already distressed at all points and on every side, after what had now happened they were seized by a fear and consternation without parallel. It was grievous enough for the state, and for every man personally, to lose so many heavy infantry, cavalry, and able-bodied troops, and to see no one left to replace them; but when they saw too that they had not enough ships in their docks, or money in the treasury, or crews for the ships, they began to despair of their salvation. They thought their enemies in Sicily would immediately sail with their fleet against Piraeus, fired up by so signal a victory; while their adversaries at home, redoubling all their preparations, would attack them vigorously by sea and land at once, aided by their own revolted confederates. Nevertheless, with such means as they had, it was decided to resist to the end — to provide timber and money, to equip a fleet as best they could, to take steps to secure their confederates and above all Euboea, to put things in the city on a more economical footing, and to elect a board of elders to advise on the state of affairs as occasion required. In short, in the way of a democracy, in the panic of the moment they were ready to be as prudent as possible.

These resolutions were carried into effect at once. Summer was now over. The following winter saw all Hellas stirring under the impression of the great Athenian disaster in Sicily. Neutrals now felt that even uninvited they ought no longer to stand aside from the war, but should volunteer to march against the Athenians, who, as they each reflected, would probably have come against them if the Sicilian campaign had succeeded. Besides, they reckoned that the war would now be short, and that it would be creditable for them to take part in it. Meanwhile the allies of the Lacedaemonians felt all more anxious than ever to see a speedy end to their heavy labours. But above all, the subjects of the Athenians showed a readiness to revolt even beyond their means, judging the circumstances with passion, and refusing even to hear that the Athenians could last out the coming summer. Beyond all this, Lacedaemon was encouraged by the near prospect of being joined in great force in the spring by her allies in Sicily, lately forced by events to acquire their own navy. With these reasons for confidence on every side, the Lacedaemonians now resolved to throw themselves without reserve into the war, considering that, once it was happily ended, they would be finally delivered from such dangers as that which would have threatened them from Athens if she had become mistress of Sicily, and that the overthrow of the Athenians would leave them in quiet enjoyment of supremacy over all Hellas.

Their king, Agis, accordingly set out at once during this winter with some troops from Decelea, levied contributions from the allies for the fleet, and turning towards the Malian Gulf exacted a sum of money from the Oetaeans by carrying off most of their cattle in reprisal for their old hostility, and, in spite of the protests and opposition of the Thessalians, forced the Achaeans of Phthiotis and the other subjects of the Thessalians in those parts to give him money and hostages, and deposited the hostages at Corinth, and tried to bring their countrymen into the confederacy. The Lacedaemonians now issued a requisition to the cities for building a hundred ships, fixing their own quota and that of the Boeotians at twenty-five each; that of the Phocians and Locrians together at fifteen; that of the Corinthians at fifteen; that of the Arcadians, Pellenians, and Sicyonians together at ten; and that of the Megarians, Troezenians, Epidaurians, and Hermionians together also at ten; and meanwhile they made every other preparation to begin hostilities by the spring.

Meanwhile the Athenians were not idle. During this same winter, as they had decided, they contributed timber and pushed on their shipbuilding, and fortified Sunium to enable their corn-ships to round it in safety, and evacuated the fort in Laconia which they had built on their way to Sicily. They also, for economy, cut down any other expenses that seemed unnecessary, and above all kept a careful watch against any revolt of their confederates.

While both parties were thus engaged, and were as intent on preparing for the war as they had been at the beginning, the Euboeans first of all sent envoys during this winter to Agis to discuss revolting from Athens. Agis accepted their proposals and sent for Alcamenes, son of Sthenelaidas, and Melanthus from Lacedaemon to take command in Euboea. They duly arrived with about three hundred Neodamodes, and Agis began to arrange for their crossing over. But meanwhile some Lesbians arrived who also wished to revolt; and as these were supported by the Boeotians, Agis was persuaded to put off action in the matter of Euboea, and made arrangements for the revolt of the Lesbians, giving them Alcamenes — who was to have sailed to Euboea — as governor, and himself promising them ten ships, with the Boeotians promising the same number. All this was done without instructions from home, since Agis, while at Decelea with the army he commanded, had power to send troops to whatever quarter he pleased and to levy men and money. During this period, one might say, the allies obeyed him much more than they did the Lacedaemonians in the city, since the force he had with him made him feared at once wherever he went. While Agis was engaged with the Lesbians, the Chians and Erythraeans, who were also ready to revolt, applied not to him but at Lacedaemon, where they arrived accompanied by an ambassador from Tissaphernes, the commander of King Darius, son of Artaxerxes, in the maritime districts. He invited the Peloponnesians to come over and promised to maintain their army. The King had lately called on him for the tribute from his government, on which he was in arrears, being unable to raise it from the Hellenic towns because of the Athenians; and he therefore reckoned that by weakening the Athenians he would get the tribute paid more easily, and would also draw the Lacedaemonians into alliance with the King; and by this means, as the King had ordered him, take alive or dead Amorges, the bastard son of Pissuthnes, who was in rebellion on the coast of Caria.

While the Chians and Tissaphernes were thus joining in pursuit of the same object, about the same time Calligeitus, son of Laophon, a Megarian, and Timagoras, son of Athenagoras, a Cyzicene — both of them exiles from their countries and living at the court of Pharnabazus, son of Pharnaces — arrived at Lacedaemon on a mission from Pharnabazus, to procure a fleet for the Hellespont. By this means, if possible, he too might secure the object of Tissaphernes’ ambition: cause the cities in his own government to revolt from the Athenians and so get the tribute, and through his own agency obtain for the King the alliance of the Lacedaemonians.

With the emissaries of Pharnabazus and Tissaphernes negotiating separately, a keen competition now ensued at Lacedaemon over whether a fleet and army should be sent first to Ionia and Chios, or to the Hellespont. The Lacedaemonians, however, decidedly favoured the Chians and Tissaphernes, who were seconded by Alcibiades, the family friend of Endius, one of the ephors for that year. (This is in fact how their family got its Laconic name, Alcibiades being the family name of Endius.) Even so, the Lacedaemonians first sent to Chios Phrynis, one of the Perioeci, to see whether they had as many ships as they said, and whether their city generally was as great as was reported. On his bringing word back that they had been told the truth, they immediately entered into alliance with the Chians and Erythraeans, and voted to send them forty ships, since there were already, according to the Chians’ statement, no fewer than sixty on the island. At first the Lacedaemonians meant to send ten of these forty themselves, with Melanchridas as their admiral; but afterwards, an earthquake having occurred, they sent Chalcideus instead of Melanchridas, and instead of the ten ships equipped only five in Laconia. So the winter ended, and with it ended the nineteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

At the beginning of the next summer the Chians were urging that the fleet should be sent off, fearing that the Athenians, from whom all these embassies were kept secret, might find out what was going on; and the Lacedaemonians at once sent three Spartans to Corinth to haul the ships across the Isthmus from the other sea to the Athens-side as quickly as possible, and to order them all to sail to Chios — those Agis was equipping for Lesbos not excepted. The number of ships from the allied states was thirty-nine in all.

Meanwhile Calligeitus and Timagoras did not join, on Pharnabazus’ behalf, in the expedition to Chios or contribute the money — twenty-five talents — they had brought with them to help dispatch a force, but decided to sail later with another force on their own. Agis, on the other hand, seeing the Lacedaemonians bent on going to Chios first, came round to their view; and the allies assembled at Corinth and held a council, in which they decided to sail first to Chios under the command of Chalcideus, who was equipping the five ships in Laconia; then to Lesbos, under the command of Alcamenes, the same whom Agis had picked; and lastly to the Hellespont, where the command was given to Clearchus, son of Ramphias. Meanwhile they would take only half the ships across the Isthmus first, and let those sail off at once, so that the Athenians might pay less attention to the squadron departing than to those still to be carried across afterwards — since no care had been taken to keep this voyage secret, through contempt for the impotence of the Athenians, who as yet had no fleet of any consequence at sea. In line with this decision, twenty-one ships were at once carried across the Isthmus.

They were now impatient to set sail, but the Corinthians were unwilling to accompany them until they had celebrated the Isthmian festival, which fell at that time. At this Agis proposed to spare them their scruples about breaking the Isthmian truce by taking the expedition on himself. The Corinthians not consenting to this, a delay followed, during which the Athenians grew suspicious of what was being prepared at Chios. They sent Aristocrates, one of their generals, and charged the Chians with the fact, and on the Chians’ denial ordered them to send with them a contingent of ships, as faithful confederates. Seven were sent accordingly. The reason for sending the ships was that the mass of the Chians were not in on the negotiations, while the few who were in the secret did not wish to break with the multitude until they had something solid to lean on, and no longer expected the Peloponnesians to arrive given their delay.

In the meantime the Isthmian games took place, and the Athenians, who had also been invited, went to attend them, and now, seeing more clearly into the designs of the Chians, as soon as they returned to Athens took measures to prevent the fleet from putting out from Cenchreae without their knowledge. After the festival the Peloponnesians set sail with twenty-one ships for Chios, under the command of Alcamenes. The Athenians first sailed against them with an equal number, drawing off towards the open sea. The enemy, however, turned back before he had followed them far, so the Athenians returned too, not trusting the seven Chian ships among their own, and afterwards manned thirty-seven ships in all and chased him along the coast into Spiraeum, a deserted Corinthian port on the edge of the Epidaurian frontier. After losing one ship at sea, the Peloponnesians got the rest together and brought them to anchor. The Athenians now attacked not only from the sea with their fleet, but also disembarked on the coast; and a melee ensued of the most confused and violent kind, in which the Athenians disabled most of the enemy’s ships and killed Alcamenes, their commander, with the loss of a few of their own men.

After this they separated, and the Athenians, detaching enough ships to blockade those of the enemy, anchored with the rest at the islet next to it, where they proceeded to make camp, and sent to Athens for reinforcements; the Peloponnesians having been joined the day after the battle by the Corinthians, who came to help the ships, and by the other inhabitants in the area not long afterwards. Seeing the difficulty of keeping guard in a deserted place, the Peloponnesians at first thought of burning the ships, but in the end resolved to haul them up on shore and sit down and guard them with their land forces until a convenient opportunity to escape should arise. Agis, on being informed of the disaster, sent them a Spartan named Thermon. The Lacedaemonians first received the news of the fleet putting out from the Isthmus — Alcamenes having been ordered by the ephors to send off a horseman when this happened — and immediately resolved to dispatch their own five vessels under Chalcideus, with Alcibiades along with him. But while they were full of this resolve, the second piece of news came: that the fleet had taken refuge in Spiraeum. Disheartened at this first step in the Ionian war proving a failure, they laid aside the idea of sending the ships from their own country, and even wished to recall some that had already sailed.

Seeing this, Alcibiades again persuaded Endius and the other ephors to persevere in the expedition, saying that the voyage would be made before the Chians heard of the fleet’s misfortune, and that as soon as he set foot in Ionia he would, by assuring them of the weakness of the Athenians and the zeal of Lacedaemon, have no difficulty in persuading the cities to revolt, since they would readily believe his testimony. He also represented to Endius privately that it would be glorious for him to be the means of making Ionia revolt and the King become the ally of Lacedaemon, instead of leaving that honour to Agis (Agis, it must be remembered, was the enemy of Alcibiades). Endius and his colleagues thus persuaded, he put to sea with the five ships and the Lacedaemonian Chalcideus, and made all haste on the voyage.

About this time the sixteen Peloponnesian ships from Sicily, which had served through the war with Gylippus, were caught on their return off Leucadia and roughly handled by the twenty-seven Athenian ships under Hippocles, son of Menippus, on the watch for the ships from Sicily. After losing one of their number, the rest escaped from the Athenians and sailed into Corinth.

Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades seized everyone they met on their voyage to prevent news of their coming, and let them go at Corycus, the first point on the mainland they touched at. Here they were visited by some of their Chian correspondents, and being urged by them to sail up to the town without announcing their coming, they arrived suddenly before Chios. The many were amazed and confused, while the few had so arranged that the council was sitting at the time; and after speeches by Chalcideus and Alcibiades stating that many more ships were on the way, but saying nothing of the fleet being blockaded in Spiraeum, the Chians revolted from the Athenians, and the Erythraeans immediately afterwards. After this three vessels sailed over to Clazomenae and made that city revolt too; and the Clazomenians at once crossed over to the mainland and began to fortify Polichna, in order to retreat there, in case of need, from the island where they lived.

While the revolted places were all engaged in fortifying and preparing for the war, news of Chios quickly reached Athens. The Athenians thought the danger they now faced great and unmistakable, and that the rest of their allies would not consent to keep quiet after the secession of the greatest of their number. In the consternation of the moment, they at once removed the penalty attaching to anyone who proposed or put to the vote a proposal for using the thousand talents which they had jealously refused to touch throughout the whole war, and voted to use them to man a large number of ships; and to send off at once under Strombichides, son of Diotimus, the eight ships, part of the blockading fleet at Spiraeum, that had left the blockade and returned after pursuing and failing to overtake the ships with Chalcideus. These were to be followed shortly afterwards by twelve more under Thrasycles, also taken from the blockade. They also recalled the seven Chian ships forming part of their squadron blockading the fleet in Spiraeum, and giving the slaves on board their liberty, put the freemen in confinement, and quickly manned and sent out ten fresh ships to blockade the Peloponnesians in place of all those that had departed, and decided to man thirty more. Zeal was not lacking, and no effort was spared to send relief to Chios.

In the meantime Strombichides with his eight ships arrived at Samos, and, taking one Samian ship along, sailed to Teos and required them to remain quiet. Chalcideus also set sail with twenty-three ships for Teos from Chios, the land forces of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans moving along the coast to support him. Informed of this in time, Strombichides put out from Teos before their arrival, and while at sea, seeing the number of the ships from Chios, fled towards Samos, chased by the enemy. The Teians at first would not receive the land forces, but on the flight of the Athenians took them into the town. There they waited for some time for Chalcideus to return from the pursuit, and as time went on without his appearing, began themselves to demolish the wall the Athenians had built on the land side of the city of the Teians, being assisted by a few of the barbarians who had come up under the command of Stages, the lieutenant of Tissaphernes.

Meanwhile Chalcideus and Alcibiades, after chasing Strombichides into Samos, armed the crews of the ships from the Peloponnese and left them at Chios, and filling their places with substitutes from Chios and manning twenty more, sailed off to bring about the revolt of Miletus. The wish of Alcibiades, who had friends among the leading men of the Milesians, was to bring over the town before the arrival of the ships from the Peloponnese, and so, by causing the revolt of as many cities as possible with the help of the Chian power and Chalcideus, to secure the honour for the Chians, for himself and Chalcideus, and, as he had promised, for Endius who had sent them out. Not noticed until their voyage was nearly complete, they arrived a little before Strombichides and Thrasycles (who had just come with twelve ships from Athens and had joined Strombichides in the pursuit), and brought about the revolt of Miletus. The Athenians, sailing up close on their heels with nineteen ships, found Miletus closed against them and took up their station at the adjacent island of Lade. The first alliance between the King and the Lacedaemonians was now concluded, immediately on the revolt of the Milesians, by Tissaphernes and Chalcideus, and was as follows:
The Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty with the King and Tissaphernes on the following terms:

1. Whatever country or cities the King has, or the King’s ancestors had, shall be the King’s; and whatever came to the Athenians from these cities, either money or any other thing, the King and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall jointly prevent the Athenians from receiving, whether money or anything else.

2. The war with the Athenians shall be carried on jointly by the King and by the Lacedaemonians and their allies; and it shall not be lawful to make peace with the Athenians except both agree — the King on his side, and the Lacedaemonians and their allies on theirs.

3. If any revolt from the King, they shall be the enemies of the Lacedaemonians and their allies. And if any revolt from the Lacedaemonians and their allies, they shall be the enemies of the King in like manner.

Such was the alliance. After this the Chians at once manned ten more ships and sailed for Anaia, in order to gain news of those in Miletus and also to make the cities revolt. A message, however, reaching them from Chalcideus telling them to go back, and saying that Amorges was at hand with a land army, they sailed to the temple of Zeus, and there sighted ten more ships sailing up with which Diomedon had set out from Athens after Thrasycles, and fled — one ship to Ephesus, the rest to Teos. The Athenians took four of their ships empty, the men finding time to escape ashore; the rest took refuge in the city of the Teians; after which the Athenians sailed off to Samos, while the Chians put to sea with their remaining ships, accompanied by the land forces, and caused Lebedos to revolt, and after it Erae. After this both the fleet and the army returned home.

About the same time the twenty Peloponnesian ships in Spiraeum, which we left chased to land and blockaded by an equal number of Athenians, suddenly sallied out, defeated the blockading squadron, took four of their ships, and, sailing back to Cenchreae, prepared again for the voyage to Chios and Ionia. Here they were joined by Astyochus as high admiral from Lacedaemon, henceforth invested with supreme command at sea. The land forces now withdrawing from Teos, Tissaphernes went there in person with an army and completed the demolition of anything left of the wall, and so departed. Not long after his departure Diomedon arrived with ten Athenian ships and, having made an arrangement by which the Teians admitted him as they had the enemy, coasted along to Erae, and, failing in an attempt on the town, sailed back again.

About this time the rising of the commons at Samos against the upper classes took place, in concert with some Athenians who were there in three ships. The Samian commons put to death some two hundred in all of the upper classes, and banished four hundred more, and themselves took their land and houses; after which the Athenians decreed their independence, being now sure of their loyalty. The commons henceforth governed the city, excluding the landholders from any share in affairs, and forbidding any of the commons to give his daughter in marriage to them or to take a wife from them in future.

After this, during the same summer, the Chians — whose zeal continued as active as ever, and who, even without the Peloponnesians, found themselves in sufficient force to bring about the revolt of the cities, and who also wished to have as many companions in danger as possible — made an expedition with thirteen ships of their own to Lesbos. The instructions from Lacedaemon were to go to that island next, and from there to the Hellespont. Meanwhile the land forces of the Peloponnesians who were with the Chians, and of the allies on the spot, moved along the coast for Clazomenae and Cuma, under the command of Eualas, a Spartan; while the fleet under Diniadas, one of the Perioeci, first sailed up to Methymna and caused it to revolt, and, leaving four ships there, with the rest brought about the revolt of Mitylene.

In the meantime Astyochus, the Lacedaemonian admiral, set sail from Cenchreae with four ships, as he had intended, and arrived at Chios. Two days later, the Athenian ships, twenty-five in number, sailed to Lesbos under Diomedon and Leon, who had recently arrived with a reinforcement of ten ships from Athens. Late the same day Astyochus put to sea, and taking one Chian ship with him sailed to Lesbos to render what assistance he could. Arrived at Pyrrha, and from there the next day at Eresus, he there learned that Mitylene had been taken almost without a blow by the Athenians, who had sailed up and unexpectedly put into the harbour, beaten the Chian ships, and, landing and defeating the troops opposed to them, had become masters of the city. Informed of this by the Eresians and by the Chian ships left with Eubulus at Methymna, which had fled when Mitylene was taken, three of which he now fell in with — one having been taken by the Athenians — Astyochus did not go on to Mitylene, but raised and armed Eresus, and, sending the heavy infantry from his own ships by land under Eteonicus to Antissa and Methymna, himself proceeded along the coast there with the ships he had with him and with the three Chians, in the hope that the Methymnians, on seeing them, would be encouraged to persevere in their revolt. Since, however, everything went against him in Lesbos, he took up his own force and sailed back to Chios; the land forces on board, which were to have gone to the Hellespont, also being conveyed back to their different cities. After this six of the allied Peloponnesian ships at Cenchreae joined the forces at Chios. The Athenians, after restoring matters to their old state in Lesbos, set sail from there and took Polichna, the place the Clazomenians were fortifying on the mainland, and carried the inhabitants back to their town on the island, except for the authors of the revolt, who withdrew to Daphnus; and so Clazomenae became Athenian once more.

The same summer the Athenians in the twenty ships at Lade, blockading Miletus, made a landing at Panormus in Milesian territory and killed Chalcideus the Lacedaemonian commander, who had come against them with a few men. Two days later they sailed over and set up a trophy, which, since they did not control the country, was, however, pulled down by the Milesians. Meanwhile Leon and Diomedon with the Athenian fleet from Lesbos, sailing out from the Oenussae, the islets off Chios, and from their forts of Sidussa and Pteleum in the Erythraeid, and from Lesbos, carried on the war against the Chians from the ships, having on board heavy infantry from the rolls pressed to serve as marines. Landing at Cardamyle and at Bolissus, they defeated with heavy loss the Chians who took the field against them, and, devastating the places in that area, defeated the Chians again in another battle at Phanae, and in a third at Leuconium. After this the Chians ceased meeting them in the field, while the Athenians ravaged the country, which was beautifully stocked and had remained uninjured ever since the Median wars. Indeed, after the Lacedaemonians, the Chians are the only people I have known who knew how to be wise in prosperity, and who managed their city more securely the greater it grew. Nor was this revolt — in which they might seem to have erred on the side of rashness — ventured on until they had numerous and gallant allies to share the danger with them, and until they perceived that the Athenians, after the Sicilian disaster, were no longer denying the thoroughly desperate state of their affairs. And if they were caught out by one of the surprises that upset human calculations, they discovered their mistake in company with many others who, like them, believed in the speedy collapse of the Athenian power. While they were thus blockaded from the sea and plundered by land, some of the citizens undertook to bring the city over to the Athenians. Apprised of this, the authorities took no action themselves, but brought Astyochus, the admiral, from Erythrae with four ships he had with him, and considered how they could most quietly, either by taking hostages or by some other means, put an end to the conspiracy.

While the Chians were thus engaged, a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and fifteen hundred Argives (five hundred of whom were light troops furnished with armour by the Athenians), and a thousand of the allies, towards the close of the same summer sailed from Athens in forty-eight ships, some of which were transports, under the command of Phrynichus, Onomacles, and Scironides; and putting into Samos, crossed over and encamped at Miletus. At this the Milesians came out to the number of eight hundred heavy infantry, with the Peloponnesians who had come with Chalcideus, some foreign mercenaries of Tissaphernes, Tissaphernes himself and his cavalry, and engaged the Athenians and their allies. While the Argives rushed forward on their own wing with the careless contempt of men advancing against Ionians who would never stand their charge, and were defeated by the Milesians with a loss little short of three hundred men, the Athenians first defeated the Peloponnesians, and driving before them the barbarians and the rest of the army, without engaging the Milesians — who, after the rout of the Argives, retreated into the town on seeing their comrades worsted — crowned their victory by grounding their arms under the very walls of Miletus. Thus, in this battle, the Ionians on both sides defeated the Dorians: the Athenians defeating the Peloponnesians opposed to them, and the Milesians the Argives. After setting up a trophy, the Athenians prepared to draw a wall around the place, which stood on an isthmus; thinking that, if they could take Miletus, the other towns would also easily come over to them.

Meanwhile, about dusk, news reached them that the fifty-five ships from the Peloponnese and Sicily might be expected at any moment. Of these the Siceliots, urged principally by the Syracusan Hermocrates to join in delivering the finishing blow to the power of Athens, furnished twenty-two — twenty from Syracuse and two from Selinus; and the ships we left preparing in the Peloponnese being now ready, both squadrons had been entrusted to Therimenes, a Lacedaemonian, to take to Astyochus, the admiral. They now put in first at Leros, the island off Miletus, and from there, discovering that the Athenians were before the town, sailed into the Iasic Gulf, in order to learn how matters stood at Miletus. Meanwhile Alcibiades came on horseback to Teichiussa in Milesian territory, the point of the gulf where they had put in for the night, and told them of the battle, in which he had fought in person beside the Milesians and Tissaphernes, and advised them, if they did not wish to sacrifice Ionia and their cause, to fly to the relief of Miletus and prevent its investment.

Accordingly they resolved to relieve it the next morning. Meanwhile Phrynichus, the Athenian commander, had received exact intelligence about the fleet from Leros, and when his colleagues expressed a wish to keep the sea and fight it out, flatly refused either to stay himself or to let them or anyone else do so if he could help it. Where they could later contend, after full and undisturbed preparation, with exact knowledge of the enemy’s numbers and of the force they could oppose to him, he would never let the reproach of disgrace drive him into a risk that was unreasonable. It was no disgrace for an Athenian fleet to retreat when it suited them; put it as you like, it would be more disgraceful to be beaten and to expose the city not only to disgrace but to the most serious danger. After its recent misfortunes, it could hardly be justified in voluntarily taking the offensive even with the strongest force, except in case of absolute necessity; much less, then, without compulsion could it rush onto a peril of its own seeking. He told them to take up their wounded as quickly as possible, along with the troops and stores they had brought with them, and, leaving behind what they had taken from the enemy’s country in order to lighten the ships, to sail off to Samos, and there, concentrating all their ships, to attack as opportunity served. As he spoke, so he acted; and thus, not now more than afterwards, nor in this matter alone but in all that he had to do with, did Phrynichus show himself a man of sense. In this way that very evening the Athenians broke up from before Miletus, leaving their victory unfinished; and the Argives, mortified at their disaster, promptly sailed off home from Samos.

As soon as it was morning the Peloponnesians weighed anchor from Teichiussa and put into Miletus after the departure of the Athenians; they stayed one day, and the next took with them the Chian ships originally chased into port with Chalcideus, and resolved to sail back for the tackle they had put on shore at Teichiussa. On their arrival, Tissaphernes came to them with his land forces and induced them to sail to Iasus, which was held by his enemy Amorges. Accordingly they suddenly attacked and took Iasus, the inhabitants having never imagined that the ships could be other than Athenian. The Syracusans distinguished themselves most in the action. Amorges, a bastard of Pissuthnes and a rebel from the King, was taken alive and handed over to Tissaphernes to take to the King, if he chose, according to his orders. Iasus was sacked by the army, who found a very great booty there, the place being wealthy from of old. The mercenaries serving with Amorges the Peloponnesians received and enrolled in their own army without harming them, since most of them came from the Peloponnese; and they handed over the town to Tissaphernes with all the captives, bond or free, at the agreed price of one Doric stater a head; after which they returned to Miletus. Pedaritus, son of Leon, who had been sent by the Lacedaemonians to take command at Chios, they dispatched by land as far as Erythrae with the mercenaries taken from Amorges, appointing Philip to remain as governor of Miletus.

Summer was now over. The following winter, Tissaphernes put Iasus into a state of defence, and passing on to Miletus distributed a month’s pay to all the ships, as he had promised at Lacedaemon, at the rate of an Attic drachma a day for each man. In future, however, he was resolved not to give more than three obols, until he had consulted the King; if the King so ordered, he said, he would give the full drachma. However, on the protest of the Syracusan general Hermocrates (since Therimenes, not being admiral but only accompanying them in order to hand over the ships to Astyochus, made little difficulty about the pay), it was agreed that the equivalent of five ships’ pay would be added over and above the three obols a day per man — Tissaphernes paying thirty talents a month for fifty-five ships, and to the rest, for as many ships as they had beyond that number, at the same rate.

The same winter the Athenians in Samos, having been joined by thirty-five more ships from home under Charminus, Strombichides, and Euctemon, called in their squadron at Chios and all the rest, intending to blockade Miletus with their navy and to send a fleet and an army against Chios; drawing lots for the respective services. This intention they carried out: Strombichides, Onomacles, and Euctemon sailed against Chios, which fell to their lot, with thirty ships and a part of the thousand heavy infantry who had been at Miletus, in transports; while the rest remained masters of the sea with seventy-four ships at Samos and advanced on Miletus.

Meanwhile Astyochus, whom we left at Chios collecting the hostages required as a result of the conspiracy, stopped on hearing that the fleet with Therimenes had arrived and that the affairs of the league were in a more flourishing condition. Putting out to sea with ten Peloponnesian and the same number of Chian ships, after a futile attack on Pteleum, he coasted on to Clazomenae and ordered the Athenian party to remove inland to Daphnus and to join the Peloponnesians, an order in which Tamos, the King’s lieutenant in Ionia, also joined. This order being disregarded, Astyochus made an attack on the town, which was unwalled; and having failed to take it, was himself carried off by a strong gale to Phocaea and Cuma, while the rest of the ships put in at the islands next to Clazomenae — Marathussa, Pele, and Drymussa. Here they were detained eight days by the winds, and, plundering and consuming all the property of the Clazomenians stored there, put the rest on shipboard and sailed off to Phocaea and Cuma to join Astyochus.

While he was there, envoys arrived from the Lesbians, who wished to revolt again. With Astyochus they were successful; but the Corinthians and the other allies, being averse to it because of their previous failure, he weighed anchor and set sail for Chios, where they eventually arrived from different quarters, the fleet having been scattered by a storm. After this Pedaritus, whom we left marching along the coast from Miletus, arrived at Erythrae, and from there crossed over with his army to Chios, where he found also about five hundred soldiers who had been left there by Chalcideus from the five ships, with their arms. Meanwhile some Lesbians making offers to revolt, Astyochus urged on Pedaritus and the Chians that they ought to go with their ships and bring about the revolt of Lesbos, and so increase the number of their allies, or, if not successful, at any rate harm the Athenians. The Chians, however, turned a deaf ear to this, and Pedaritus flatly refused to give up the Chian ships to him.

At this Astyochus took five Corinthian and one Megarian ship, with another from Hermione, and the ships that had come with him from Laconia, and set sail for Miletus to assume his command as admiral; after telling the Chians with many threats that he would certainly not come and help them if they should be in need. At Corycus in the Erythraeid he brought to for the night; the Athenian armament sailing from Samos against Chios being separated from him only by a hill, on the other side of which it brought to, so that neither saw the other. But a letter arriving in the night from Pedaritus to say that some liberated Erythraean prisoners had come from Samos to betray Erythrae, Astyochus at once put back to Erythrae, and so just escaped falling in with the Athenians. Pedaritus sailed over to join him there; and after inquiry into the supposed treachery, finding that the whole story had been made up to procure the men’s escape from Samos, they acquitted them of the charge, and sailed away — Pedaritus to Chios, and Astyochus to Miletus as he had intended.

Meanwhile the Athenian armament sailing round Corycus fell in with three Chian men-of-war off Arginus, and gave immediate chase. A great storm coming on, the Chians with difficulty took refuge in the harbour; the three Athenian ships most forward in the pursuit were wrecked and thrown up near the city of Chios, the crews being killed or taken prisoner. The rest of the Athenian fleet took refuge in the harbour called Phoenicus, under Mount Mimas, and from there afterwards put in to Lesbos and prepared for the work of fortification.

The same winter the Lacedaemonian Hippocrates sailed out from the Peloponnese with ten Thurian ships under the command of Dorieus, son of Diagoras, and two colleagues, one Laconian and one Syracusan ship, and arrived at Cnidus, which had already revolted at the instigation of Tissaphernes. When their arrival was known at Miletus, orders came for them to leave half their squadron to guard Cnidus and with the rest to cruise round Triopium and seize all the merchant ships arriving from Egypt. Triopium is a promontory of Cnidus and sacred to Apollo. The Athenians, getting word of this, sailed from Samos and captured the six ships on watch at Triopium, the crews escaping out of them. After this the Athenians sailed into Cnidus and made an assault on the town, which was unfortified, and all but took it; and the next day assaulted it again, but with less effect, since the inhabitants had improved their defences during the night and had been reinforced by the crews escaped from the ships at Triopium. The Athenians now withdrew, and after plundering the Cnidian territory sailed back to Samos.

About the same time Astyochus came to the fleet at Miletus. The Peloponnesian camp was still plentifully supplied, being in receipt of sufficient pay, and the soldiers having still in hand the large booty taken at Iasus. The Milesians too showed great ardour for the war. Nevertheless the Peloponnesians thought the first convention with Tissaphernes, made with Chalcideus, defective and more advantageous to him than to them, and so, while Therimenes was still there, concluded another, which was as follows:
The convention of the Lacedaemonians and the allies with King Darius and the sons of the King, and with Tissaphernes, for a treaty and friendship, as follows:

1. Neither the Lacedaemonians nor the allies of the Lacedaemonians shall make war on or otherwise injure any country or cities that belong to King Darius, or did belong to his father or to his ancestors; nor shall the Lacedaemonians or the allies of the Lacedaemonians exact tribute from such cities. Nor shall King Darius or any of the King’s subjects make war on or otherwise injure the Lacedaemonians or their allies.
2. If the Lacedaemonians or their allies should require any assistance from the King, or the King from the Lacedaemonians or their allies, whatever they both agree on, they shall be right in doing.
3. Both shall jointly carry on the war against the Athenians and their allies; and if they make peace, both shall do so jointly.
4. The expense of all troops in the King’s country, sent for by the King, shall be borne by the King.

5. If any of the states comprised in this convention with the King attack the King’s country, the rest shall stop them and aid the King to the best of their power. And if any in the King’s country, or in the countries under the King’s rule, attack the country of the Lacedaemonians or their allies, the King shall stop it and help them to the best of his power.

After this convention, Therimenes handed over the fleet to Astyochus, sailed off in a small boat, and was lost. The Athenian armament had now crossed over from Lesbos to Chios, and being master by sea and land, began to fortify Delphinium, a place naturally strong on the land side, with more than one harbour, and not far from the city of Chios. Meanwhile the Chians remained inactive. Already defeated in so many battles, they were now also at odds among themselves; the execution of the party of Tydeus, son of Ion, by Pedaritus on the charge of Atticism, followed by the forcible imposition of an oligarchy on the rest of the city, had made them suspicious of one another; and they therefore thought neither themselves nor the mercenaries under Pedaritus a match for the enemy. They sent, however, to Miletus to beg Astyochus to assist them, which he refused to do; and he was accordingly denounced at Lacedaemon by Pedaritus as a traitor. Such was the state of the Athenian affairs at Chios; while their fleet at Samos kept sailing out against the enemy at Miletus, until they found that he would not accept their challenge, and then withdrew again to Samos and remained quiet.

In the same winter the twenty-seven ships equipped by the Lacedaemonians for Pharnabazus through the agency of the Megarian Calligeitus and the Cyzicene Timagoras put out from the Peloponnese and sailed for Ionia about the time of the solstice, under the command of Antisthenes, a Spartan. With them the Lacedaemonians also sent eleven Spartans as advisers to Astyochus, Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, being among them. Arrived at Miletus, their orders were to aid in generally overseeing the good conduct of the war; to send off the above ships, or a greater or smaller number, to the Hellespont to Pharnabazus, if they thought proper, appointing Clearchus, son of Ramphias, who sailed with them, to the command; and further, if they thought proper, to make Antisthenes admiral, dismissing Astyochus, whom Pedaritus’ letters had caused to be regarded with suspicion. Sailing accordingly from Malea across the open sea, the squadron touched at Melos and there fell in with ten Athenian ships, three of which they took empty and burned. After this, fearing that the Athenian ships escaped from Melos might, as they did in fact, give information of their approach to the Athenians at Samos, they sailed to Crete, and having lengthened their voyage by way of precaution, made land at Caunus in Asia, from where, considering themselves safe, they sent a message to the fleet at Miletus for an escort along the coast.

Meanwhile the Chians and Pedaritus, undeterred by the slowness of Astyochus, went on sending messengers urging him to come with all the fleet to assist them against their besiegers, and not to leave the greatest of the allied states in Ionia to be shut up by sea and overrun and pillaged by land. There were more slaves at Chios than in any one other city except Lacedaemon, and being also, because of their numbers, punished more rigorously when they offended, most of them, when they saw the Athenian armament firmly established on the island in a fortified position, immediately deserted to the enemy, and through their knowledge of the country did the greatest mischief. The Chians therefore urged on Astyochus that it was his duty to assist them while there was still hope and possibility of stopping the enemy’s progress, while Delphinium was still in the process of fortification and unfinished, and before the completion of a higher rampart that was being added to protect the camp and fleet of their besiegers. Astyochus now saw that the allies also wished it, and prepared to go, in spite of his intention to the contrary because of the threat referred to.

In the meantime news came from Caunus of the arrival of the twenty-seven ships with the Lacedaemonian commissioners; and Astyochus, putting everything else aside for the duty of convoying a fleet of that importance — both to be more able to command the sea, and to ensure the safe passage of the Lacedaemonians sent as spies on his behaviour — at once gave up going to Chios and set sail for Caunus. As he coasted along he landed at Meropid Cos and sacked the city, which was unfortified and had recently been laid in ruins by an earthquake, by far the greatest in living memory; and, since the inhabitants had fled to the mountains, overran the country and made booty of all it contained, letting the free men go, however. From Cos, arriving at Cnidus by night, he was urged by the representations of the Cnidians not to disembark the sailors, but to sail as he was straight against the twenty Athenian ships which, under Charminus, one of the commanders at Samos, were on the watch for the very twenty-seven ships from the Peloponnese which Astyochus was himself sailing to join; the Athenians at Samos having heard from Melos of their approach, and Charminus being on the lookout off Syme, Chalce, Rhodes, and Lycia, since he now heard that they were at Caunus.

Astyochus accordingly sailed as he was to Syme, before he was heard of, in the hope of catching the enemy somewhere out at sea. Rain, however, and foggy weather caught him and caused his ships to straggle and get into disorder in the dark. In the morning his fleet had parted company and was most of it still straggling round the island, with only the left wing in sight of Charminus and the Athenians, who took it for the squadron they were watching for from Caunus, and hastily put out against it with only part of their twenty ships. Attacking immediately, they sank three ships and disabled others, and had the advantage in the action until the main body of the fleet unexpectedly came in sight, when they were surrounded on every side. They took to flight, and after losing six ships escaped with the rest to Teutlussa, or Beet Island, and from there to Halicarnassus. After this the Peloponnesians put in to Cnidus, and being joined by the twenty-seven ships from Caunus, sailed all together and set up a trophy at Syme, then returned to anchor at Cnidus.

As soon as the Athenians knew of the sea-fight, they sailed with all the ships at Samos to Syme, and, without attacking or being attacked by the fleet at Cnidus, took the ships’ tackle left at Syme, and touching at Lorymi on the mainland sailed back to Samos. Meanwhile the Peloponnesian ships, being now all at Cnidus, underwent such repairs as were needed; while the eleven Lacedaemonian commissioners conferred with Tissaphernes, who had come to meet them, on the points that did not satisfy them in the past transactions, and on the best and mutually most advantageous way of conducting the war in future. The severest critic of the present state of things was Lichas, who said that neither of the treaties could stand — neither that of Chalcideus nor that of Therimenes; it being monstrous that the King should at this date pretend to possession of all the country formerly ruled by himself or by his ancestors — a pretension that implicitly put back under the yoke all the islands, Thessaly, Locris, and everything as far as Boeotia, and made the Lacedaemonians give the Hellenes a Median master instead of liberty. He therefore invited Tissaphernes to conclude another and a better treaty, since they certainly would not recognize those existing and did not want any of his pay on such conditions. This offended Tissaphernes so much that he went off in a rage without settling anything.
